newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia to push on with reforms despite parliament.
newsitem.headline: Russia to push on with reforms despite parliament.

text.p: The Russian government vowed to press on with economic reforms aimed at restoring the state's finances despite dogged opposition from parliament, which threw out a final batch of bills on Tuesday before going on holiday.

"With or without the Duma, with or without its desire to help, all the necessary solutions will be found in any case," First Deputy Prime Minister Anatoly Chubais told reporters. "On no account are we going to wait for manna from heaven."

"If the Duma is not able to take decisions...we will live by our own decisions," he said. Government experts were already looking at ways to implement immediate cost savings and welfare cuts, which could be imposed by presidential decree.

Visibly irritated by the communist-dominated State Duma lower house's failure to accept any compromise on two out of three key pieces of legislation in the past week, Chubais accused the deputies of being incapable of contributing to policy-making but stopped short of demanding new elections.

The Duma conditionally approved a new tax code last week but on Monday rejected a bill to slash 1997 spending by a fifth after a drop in tax revenue and on Tuesday threw out most of a package of measures to cut back on Soviet-era welfare benefits the government says it can no longer afford.
"If the Duma does not take on responsibilities, it makes one doubt whether it is capable of working," Chubais said.

"Out of three questions, the Duma completely failed to take a decision on two of them...It suggests the majority in the Duma is not capable of taking political responsibility to the extent demanded today."
However, asked if the government wanted President Boris Yeltsin to dissolve the uncooperative lower chamber, Chubais stressed that such a decision was up to the head of state.
"Extreme options should be applied only in extreme cases," he said, without elaborating.
Regular recent threats of dissolution form part of a delicate tango between the government, backed by Yeltsin and his huge constitutional powers, and the relatively weak parliament.

The prospect of new elections, two years early, discomfits sitting deputies. But the Kremlin seems unlikely to go as far as dissolving the Duma since voters are still unhappy with the economy and are unlikely to return a more cooperative chamber.

Duma speaker Gennady Seleznyov, a communist, told Interfax news agency that parliament would not be pushed around by ministers who insisted on continuing their "monetary course" without thought for the sufferings of ordinary people.
"The State Duma is not a political institution you can deal with using the rhetoric of ultimatums," Seleznyov said.

Ministers in the youthful new government, formed by Yeltsin exactly 100 days ago to push through new market reforms, say the Duma is failing to address reality. The spending cut legislation would do little more than regularise the current situation, since the state is simply failing to pay many of its bills.
Chubais said the government would meet its pledge to pay off arrears on old age pensions by the end of this month and would take further steps to ensure they did not build up again.

Foreign financial analysts welcomed the government's determination but warned that the undoubted sufferings of ordinary Russians after six years of post-Soviet reforms meant ministers still had a tough job on their hands.
"The government's going to go ahead with the cuts anyway -- Chubais has said if the money's not there, it can't be spent," said Eastern Europe analyst Charles Robertson.
"But there are still some dangers here -- at what point will the population get upset about wage arrears and lose faith in democracy?"
